title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
• Secure domain controllers (DCs). Malicious actors often target and use DCs as a staging
point to spread ransomware network wide. To secure DCs:
o Use the latest version of Windows Server supported by your organization on DCs.
Newer versions of Windows Server OS have more security features, including for Active
Directory, integrated. For guidance on configuring available security features refer to
Microsoft’s Best Practices for Securing Active Directory.
 The authoring organizations recommend using Windows Server 2019 or greater
and Windows 10 or greater as they have security features, such as LSASS
protections with Windows Credential Guard, Windows Defender, and
Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI), not included in older operating system
o Ensure that DCs are regularly patched. Apply patches for critical vulnerabilities as soon
as possible.
o Use open-source penetration testing tools, such as BloodHound or PingCastle, to verify
domain controller security.
o Ensure that minimal software or agents are installed on DCs because these can be
leveraged to run arbitrary code on the system.
o Restrict access to DCs to the Administrators group. Users within this group should be
limited and have separate accounts used for day-to-day operations with nonadministrative permissions. For more information, refer to Microsoft’s Securing Active
Directory Administrative Groups and Accounts.
 The designated admin accounts should only be used for admin purposes. Ensure
that checking emails, web browsing, or other high-risk activities are not
performed on DCs.
o Configure DC host firewalls to prevent internet access. Usually, DCs do not need direct
internet access. Servers with internet connectivity can be used to pull necessary
updates in lieu of allowing internet access for DCs.
o Implement a privileged access management (PAM) solution on DCs to assist in
managing and monitoring privileged access.

Usually, DCs do not need direct
internet access. Servers with internet connectivity can be used to pull necessary
updates in lieu of allowing internet access for DCs.
o Implement a privileged access management (PAM) solution on DCs to assist in
managing and monitoring privileged access. PAM solutions can also log and alert usage
to detect unusual activity.
o Consider disabling or limiting NTLM and WDigest Authentication, if possible. Include
their use as criteria for prioritizing upgrading legacy systems or for segmenting the
network. Instead use modern federation protocols (e.g., SAML, OIDC or Kerberos) for
authentication with AES-256 bit
encryptionhttps://cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/2022_00092_CISA_CPG_Repo
rt_508c.pdf. If NTLM must be enabled:
 Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) to prevent some NTLM-
relay attacks. For more information, refer to Microsoft Mitigating NTLM Relay
Attacks on Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS).
 Enable NTLM auditing to ensure that only NTLMv2 responses are sent across
the network. Measures should be taken to ensure that LM and NTLM responses
are refused, if possible.

title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
o Enable additional protections for LSA Authentication to prevent code injection capable of
acquiring credentials from the system. Prior to enabling these protections, run audits
against lsass.exe to ensure an understanding of the programs that will be affected by
the enabling of this protection.
• Retain and adequately secure logs from network devices, local hosts, and cloud
services. This supports triage and remediation of cybersecurity events. Logs can be analyzed
to determine the impact of events and ascertain if an incident has occurred [CPG 2.T].
o Set up centralized log management using a security information and event management
tool [CPG 2.U]. This enables an organization to correlate logs from both network and
host security devices. By reviewing logs from multiple sources, an organization can
triage an individual event and determine its impact to the organization.
o Maintain and back up logs for critical systems for a minimum of one year, if possible.
• Establish a security baseline of normal network traffic and tune network appliances to
detect anomalous behavior. Tune host-based products to detect anomalous binaries, lateral
movement, and persistence techniques.
o Consider using business transaction logging—such as logging activity related to specific
or critical applications—for behavioral analytics.
• Conduct regular assessments to ensure processes and procedures are up to date and can be
followed by security staff and end users.
• Enable tracking prevention to limit the vectors that ad networks and trackers can use to track
user information.
• Enable website typo protection to limit the possibility of logging onto spoofed websites or
other potential malicious links that could compromise a browser.
• Enable browser-based AV for active scanning while browsing as an added layer of defense.
• Block website notifications by default to limit site’s ability to track user data that can be
exploited.

title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
Part 2: Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist
Should your organization be a victim of
ransomware, follow your approved IRP. The
authoring organizations strongly recommend
responding by using the following checklist.
Be sure to move through the first three
steps in sequence.
Detection and Analysis
Refer to the best practices and references
below to help manage the risk posed by
ransomware and support your organization’s
coordinated and efficient response to a
ransomware incident. Apply these practices
to the greatest extent possible based on
availability of organizational resources.
 1. Determine which systems were
impacted, and immediately isolate
them.
□ If several systems or subnets
appear impacted, take the network offline at the switch level. It may not be feasible to
disconnect individual systems during an incident.
□ Prioritize isolating critical systems that are essential to daily operations.
□ If taking the network temporarily offline is not immediately possible, locate the network
cable (e.g., ethernet) and unplug affected devices from the network or remove them
from Wi-Fi to contain the infection.
□ For cloud resources, take a snapshot of volumes to get a point in time copy for reviewing
later for forensic investigation.
□ After an initial compromise, malicious actors may monitor your organization’s activity or
communications to understand if their actions have been detected. Isolate systems in a
coordinated manner and use out-of-band communication methods such as phone calls
to avoid tipping off actors that they have been discovered and that mitigation actions are
being undertaken. Not doing so could cause actors to move laterally to preserve their
access or deploy ransomware widely prior to networks being taken offline.
 2. Power down devices if you are unable to disconnect them from the network to avoid
further spread of the ransomware infection.
Note: This step will prevent your organization from maintaining ransomware infection artifacts
and potential evidence stored in volatile memory.
section: Part 2: Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist

title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
Power down devices if you are unable to disconnect them from the network to avoid
further spread of the ransomware infection.
Note: This step will prevent your organization from maintaining ransomware infection artifacts
and potential evidence stored in volatile memory. It should be carried out only if it is not
possible to temporarily shut down the network or disconnect affected hosts from the
network using other means.
The authoring organizations do not recommend
paying ransom. Paying ransom will not ensure your
data is decrypted, that your systems or data will no
longer be compromised, or that your data will not be
leaked.
Additionally, paying ransoms may pose sanctions
risks. For information on potential sanctions risks,
see U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of
Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) memorandum from
September 2021, Updated Advisory on Potential
Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware
Payments. The updated advisory states that
Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
would consider 'mitigating factors' in related
enforcement actions. Contact your local FBI field
office, in consultation with OFAC, for guidance on
mitigating penalty factors after an attack.
section: Part 2: Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist

title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
 3. Triage impacted systems for restoration and recovery.
□ Identify and prioritize critical systems for restoration on a clean network and confirm the
nature of data housed on impacted systems.
 Prioritize restoration and recovery based on a predefined critical asset list that
includes information systems critical for health and safety, revenue generation, or
other critical services, as well as systems they depend on.
□ Keep track of systems and devices that are not perceived to be impacted so they can be
deprioritized for restoration and recovery. This enables your organization to get back to
business in a more efficient manner.
 4. Examine existing organizational detection or prevention systems (e.g., antivirus, EDR,
IDS, Intrusion Prevention System) and logs. Doing so can highlight evidence of additional
systems or malware involved in earlier stages of the attack.
□ Look for evidence of precursor “dropper” malware, such as Bumblebee, Dridex, Emotet,
QakBot, or Anchor. A ransomware event may be evidence of a previous, unresolved
network compromise.
 Operators of these advanced malware variants will often sell access to a
network. Malicious actors will sometimes use this access to exfiltrate data and
then threaten to release the data publicly before ransoming the network to further
extort the victim and pressure them into paying.
 Malicious actors often drop ransomware variants to obscure post-compromise
activity. Care must be taken to identify such dropper malware before rebuilding
from backups to prevent continuing compromises.
 5. Confer with your team to develop and document an initial understanding of what has
occurred based on initial analysis.
 6.

title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
Care must be taken to identify such dropper malware before rebuilding
from backups to prevent continuing compromises.
 5. Confer with your team to develop and document an initial understanding of what has
occurred based on initial analysis.
 6. Initiate threat hunting activities.
□ For enterprise environments, check for:
 Newly created AD accounts or accounts with escalated privileges and recent
activity related to privileged accounts such as Domain Admins.
 Anomalous VPN device logins or other suspicious logins.
 Endpoint modifications that may impair backups, shadow copy, disk journaling,
or boot configurations. Look for anomalous usage of built-in Windows tools such
as bcdedit.exe, fsutil.exe (deletejournal), vssadmin.exe, wbadmin.exe,
and wmic.exe (shadowcopy or shadowstorage). Misuse of these tools is a
common ransomware technique to inhibit system recovery.
 Signs of the presence of Cobalt Strike beacon/client. Cobalt Strike is a
commercial penetration testing software suite. Malicious actors often name
Cobalt Strike Windows processes with the same names as legitimate Windows
processes to obfuscate their presence and complicate investigations.
section: Part 2: Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist

title: #StopRansomware Guide
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and National Security Agency (NSA), with contributing partners
text:
 Signs of any unexpected usage of remote monitoring and management (RMM)
software (including portable executables that are not installed). RMM software is
commonly used by malicious actors to maintain persistence.
 Any unexpected PowerShell execution or use of PsTools suite.
 Signs of enumeration of AD and/or LSASS credentials being dumped (e.g.,
Mimikatz, Sysinternals ProcDump, or NTDSutil.exe).
 Signs of unexpected endpoint-to-endpoint (including servers) communications,
for example, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) poisoning of an endpoint or
command and control traffic relayed between endpoints.
 Potential signs of data being exfiltrated from the network, which may include:
• Abnormal amount of data outgoing over any port. Open source software
can tunnel data over various ports and protocols. For example,
ransomware actors have used Chisel to tunnel Secure Shell (SSH) over
HTTPS port 443. Ransomware actors have also used Cloudflared to
abuse Cloudflare tunnels to tunnel communications over HTTPS.
• Presence of Rclone, Rsync, and various web-based file storage services,
and FTP/SFTP, which are common tools for data exfiltration (and also
used by threat actors to implant malware/tools on affected networks.)
 Newly created services, unexpected scheduled tasks, unexpected software
installed, unusual files created, legitimate processes with unexpected child
processes, etc.
□ For cloud environments:
 Enable tools to detect and prevent modifications to IAM, network security, and
data protection resources.
 Use automation to detect common issues (e.g., disabling features, introduction of
new firewall rules) and take automated actions as soon as they occur.

title: #StopRansomware Guide

text:
Containment and Eradication
If no initial mitigation actions appear possible:
 9. Take a system image and memory
capture of a sample of affected devices
(e.g., workstations, servers, virtual
servers, and cloud servers). Collect any
relevant logs as well as samples of any
“precursor” malware binaries and associated
observables or indicators of compromise
(e.g., suspected command and control IP
addresses, suspicious registry entries, or
other relevant files detected). The contacts
below may be able to assist you in
performing these tasks.
□ Preserve evidence that is highly
volatile in nature—or limited in
retention—to prevent loss or
tampering (e.g., system memory,
Windows Security logs, data in firewall log buffers).

 10. Consult federal law enforcement, even if mitigation actions are possible, regarding
possible decryptors available, as security researchers may have discovered encryption flaws
for some ransomware variants and released decryption or other types of tools.
To continue taking steps to contain and mitigate the incident:
 11. Research trusted guidance (e.g., published by sources such as the U.S. Government,
MS-ISAC, or a reputable security vendor) for the particular ransomware variant and follow any
additional recommended steps to identify and contain systems or networks that are confirmed to
be impacted.
□ Kill or disable the execution of known ransomware binaries; this will minimize damage
and impact to your systems. Delete other known associated registry values and files.

 12. Identify the systems and accounts involved in the initial breach. This can include email
accounts.

 13. Based on the breach or compromise details determined above, contain associated
systems that may be used for further or continued unauthorized access. Breaches often

encryption quick identification steps.
□ Review Computer Management > Sessions and Open Files lists on associated servers
to determine the user or system accessing those files.
□ Review file properties of encrypted files or ransom notes to identify specific users that
may be associated with file ownership.
□ Review the TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager event log to check for
successful RDP network connections.
□ Review the Windows Security log, SMB event logs, and related logs that may identify
significant authentication or access events.
□ Run packet capture software, such as Wireshark, on the impacted server with a filter to
identify IP addresses involved in actively writing or renaming files (e.g., smb2.filename
contains cryptxxx).
 15. Conduct extended analysis to identify outside-in and inside-out persistence
mechanisms.
□ Outside-in persistence may include authenticated access to external systems via rogue
accounts, backdoors on perimeter systems, exploitation of external vulnerabilities, etc.
□ Inside-out persistence may include malware implants on the internal network or a variety
of living-off-the-land style modifications (e.g., use of commercial penetration testing tools
like Cobalt Strike; use of PsTools suite, including PsExec, to remotely install and control
malware and gather information regarding—or perform remote management of—
Windows systems; use of PowerShell scripts).
□ Identification may involve deployment of EDR solutions, audits of local and domain
accounts, examination of data found in centralized logging systems, or deeper forensic
analysis of specific systems once movement within the environment has been mapped
out.

Phishing Incident Response Procedure (SYNTHETIC)
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. Document Control
This procedure has document ID AIT-IR-PR-001 and is currently at version 2.3. The procedure is owned by the AIT-CSIRT and became effective on 1 March 2026.

2. Reporting
Staff and students report suspicious emails with the Report Phish button in the mail client or by forwarding the message as an attachment to phish-report@ait.example. Forwarding the message as an attachment is required so that the original email headers are preserved.

3. Triage
A Tier 1 analyst must acknowledge each phishing report within 15 minutes during business hours, which are 08:00 to 18:00 local time from Monday to Friday. Outside business hours the acknowledgement target is 60 minutes.
Within 30 minutes of acknowledgement, the analyst classifies the report as spam, phishing, spearphishing, or business email compromise. Attachments are detonated in the DetonateBox sandbox with a timeout of 180 seconds.

4. Containment
MailShield automatically removes a message from all mailboxes when five or more users report it within 20 minutes. Tier 2 adds confirmed malicious domains to the proxy blocklist within 2 hours.
If a user entered credentials on a phishing page, the password must be reset and all active sessions revoked within 1 hour. The affected user must then re-register multi-factor authentication.

5. Communication and Escalation
If a campaign reaches more than 25 recipients, the CSIRT sends a campaign advisory to all staff within 4 hours. The Incident Manager is engaged immediately when three or more members of the executive group are targeted.

5. Communication and Escalation
If a campaign reaches more than 25 recipients, the CSIRT sends a campaign advisory to all staff within 4 hours. The Incident Manager is engaged immediately when three or more members of the executive group are targeted.
Confirmed credential submission is ticketed as priority P2, while a report with no user interaction is ticketed as priority P3. Tickets use the prefix IR- followed by a sequence number.

6. Evidence and Metrics
The original message is stored as an .eml file for 18 months. The target mean time to remove a malicious email from all mailboxes is 45 minutes. Users who reported a false positive are told the outcome within 1 business day.

7. Roles and Responsibilities
Tier 1 analysts receive and triage reports and open the ticket. Tier 2 analysts investigate confirmed campaigns, update the proxy blocklist, and coordinate with the mail administrators. The Incident Manager takes over when a campaign involves several departments or senior staff, and the Communications Office reviews every advisory before it is sent to all staff.

8. Definitions
Phishing is a fraudulent message that tries to trick the recipient into revealing credentials or running malicious content. Spearphishing is phishing aimed at a specific person or group, usually with personal details that make the message look credible. Business email compromise is a fraud in which an attacker impersonates a manager or supplier to request payments or data. A campaign is a set of related messages sent by the same attacker.

9. Related Documents
This procedure is used together with the Account Compromise Response Procedure (AIT-IR-AC-004) and the EDR Alert Triage Procedure (AIT-IR-ED-010).

An outbreak is declared when SentryEDR detects the same malware family on three or more hosts within 30 minutes. The on-duty CSIRT lead appoints an Outbreak Lead within 10 minutes of the declaration.

Workstations are isolated with the SentryEDR contain-host action within 15 minutes of declaration. Servers are isolated only after approval from the on-call system owner, which must be obtained within 20 minutes. If the system owner cannot be reached, the CSIRT lead may authorize isolation.

Status updates go to stakeholders every 2 hours during an active outbreak. A host returns to service after two consecutive clean full scans and 24 hours of monitoring. An outbreak is closed after 72 hours without new detections.

2. DECISION AUTHORITY

The CISO may approve isolation of the entire campus network when 50 or more hosts show encryption activity or when any domain controller is affected.

No staff member may contact the attackers; any communication is handled only through legal counsel. A ransom payment requires written approval from both the Board Risk Committee and legal counsel.

AIT-CSIRT notifies law enforcement within 24 hours of confirming a ransomware incident.

3. EVIDENCE HANDLING

Cloud volumes are snapshotted before they are isolated. Ransom notes are photographed and hashed before any cleanup.

VaultSafe copies immutable backups to the offline vault every night at 02:00. Backups in the offline vault are retained for 35 days.

Tier 0 identity services are restored first, with a recovery time objective of 12 hours. The ERP system is restored next, with a recovery time objective of 48 hours. Public decryptor repositories are checked before any restore decision.

5. CREDENTIAL RESET

All privileged credentials are rotated before systems are reconnected. The KRBTGT account password is reset twice, with at least 10 hours between the two resets.

6. COORDINATION

The war room is Room B-204 and the out-of-band bridge is extension 7000.

Account Compromise Response Procedure (SYNTHETIC)
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. Document Control
This procedure has document ID AIT-IR-AC-004 and is at version 2.0.

2. Indicators
Impossible travel is flagged when two sign-ins occur more than 500 kilometres apart within 60 minutes. MFA fatigue is suspected when a user receives 10 or more push prompts within 5 minutes. A new inbox rule that forwards mail to an external address is treated as a compromise indicator.

3. Preventive Controls
Accounts are locked for 15 minutes after 5 failed sign-in attempts. AIT requires a minimum password length of 14 characters.

4. Containment
Confirmed compromised accounts are disabled within 15 minutes of confirmation. All refresh tokens and active sessions are revoked at the same time. Malicious inbox rules and delegated access are removed before the account is re-enabled.
Compromise of a privileged account is ticketed as priority P1 and the CISO is notified within 30 minutes. Secrets of compromised service accounts are rotated within 4 hours with approval of the service owner.

5. Investigation
Analysts review sign-in logs for the preceding 30 days. Sign-in logs are retained for 400 days.

6. Recovery and Follow-up
Student accounts are re-enabled only after identity verification at the Help Desk, in person or by video. The user completes the 20-minute Account Hygiene micro-training within 7 days. HR is informed if an employee is suspected of deliberate misuse.

7. Roles and Responsibilities
Tier 1 analysts confirm alerts from the identity platform and disable accounts. Tier 2 analysts review sign-in logs and mailbox rules.

2. DETECTION THRESHOLDS

Normal traffic averages 2.4 Gbps. A warning alert is raised at 6 Gbps sustained for 5 minutes. The critical threshold is 12 Gbps.

3. MITIGATION

Tier 2 enables WAF Under Attack mode when the warning threshold is reached. The ISP scrubbing service from NorthLink is activated by calling the 24x7 hotline at extension 7010.

DNS record TTLs are lowered to 300 seconds in preparation for traffic redirection. The login portal is limited to 100 requests per second per client IP address. Geo-blocking requires CISO approval and may last at most 24 hours.

Service restoration priority is the learning portal first, then email, then the library system. The status page is updated within 20 minutes of a confirmed attack.

5. ANALYSIS AND ESCALATION

Analysts capture 15-minute packet samples for later analysis. The Incident Manager is engaged when an outage exceeds 30 minutes.

6. RESTRICTIONS AND REPORTING

Retaliation against attacking systems, known as hack-back, is prohibited. An after-action report is due within 5 business days.

7. ROLES

The Network Team operates the edge routers and requests traffic scrubbing from the ISP. Tier 2 analysts tune the web application firewall during an attack.

text:
Log Management and Retention Policy (SYNTHETIC)
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. Purpose and Scope
Logs are the primary source of evidence when AIT investigates a security incident. Without reliable logs, analysts cannot reconstruct what an attacker did, which accounts were used, or which data was touched. This policy defines which logs must be collected, how long they are kept, and who may read them. The policy has document ID AIT-IR-LG-006 and is at version 1.1.
It applies to all servers, network devices, cloud tenants, and managed endpoints owned by AIT. Personally owned devices that only use the guest wireless network are out of scope.

2. Collection
All in-scope systems forward logs to the LogVault SIEM using syslog over TLS on port 6514. Systems that cannot use TLS must forward through an approved relay in the same network segment, and the relay must be listed in the asset inventory.
All timestamps are recorded in UTC, which avoids confusion when events from several time zones are correlated. System clocks are synchronized with NTP and must not drift by more than 2 seconds. Windows hosts must enable PowerShell script block logging so that script activity can be reconstructed later.

3. Retention
Retention periods depend on the log type and are set to balance investigation needs against storage cost. Authentication logs are kept for 12 months in hot storage and then for 3 years in the archive. Firewall logs are kept for 180 days, web proxy logs for 120 days, and DNS query logs for 90 days.
Endpoint detection telemetry is kept for 60 days because of its high volume. Privileged access audit logs are kept for 5 years.

title: Log Management and Retention Policy (SYNTHETIC)
publisher: APA Project (synthetic document)
text:
Firewall logs are kept for 180 days, web proxy logs for 120 days, and DNS query logs for 90 days.
Endpoint detection telemetry is kept for 60 days because of its high volume. Privileged access audit logs are kept for 5 years. Expired logs are securely deleted within 30 days of reaching the end of their retention period.

4. Integrity and Access
Log files are protected with SHA-256 hashes computed every hour, so that any later modification can be detected. Hash values are stored on a separate system that the log administrators cannot modify.
Only members of the SOC and the Audit Office may read raw logs. The SOC Manager approves access requests within 2 business days. Every access to raw logs is itself logged.

5. Monitoring of the Logging Service
A log source that sends no events for 15 minutes triggers a silent-source alert, because a source that goes quiet may indicate tampering or a failed forwarder. LogVault ingests about 450 GB per day on average and is sized for 600 GB per day. Storage utilization above 80 percent triggers a capacity review.

6. Governance
The SOC Manager reviews this policy every 12 months. Exceptions are valid for at most 90 days and require written approval from the CISO. Every exception is recorded in the policy exception register.

7. Roles and Responsibilities
The SOC Manager owns this policy and the LogVault service. The Infrastructure Team configures log forwarding on servers and network devices. The Audit Office may request additional log sources when an audit requires them, and the CISO resolves disagreements about retention periods. System owners are responsible for confirming that new systems send logs before they go live.

8. Definitions
A log source is any system, application, or device that generates events which are sent to LogVault. Hot storage is fast storage that supports interactive searches.

SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. Purpose and Scope
This standard sets how often AIT scans its own systems for vulnerabilities and how quickly findings must be fixed. The goal is to reduce the time during which a known weakness can be abused. It has document ID AIT-IR-VM-007 and is at version 2.1. It covers all servers, workstations, network devices, and internet-facing assets managed by AIT.

2. Scanning
Authenticated vulnerability scans run weekly on all servers and monthly on workstations. Internet-facing assets are scanned daily. Scans originate only from the scanner subnet 10.20.30.0/24, so that defenders can distinguish approved scans from hostile scanning.
Scanning of production servers is allowed only between 22:00 and 05:00 to limit the effect on users. Assets that are missing from the asset inventory for more than 14 days are flagged to the asset owner. Scan results are imported into TrackDesk, where each finding receives a ticket with the prefix VM-.

3. Remediation Deadlines
Deadlines are based on the CVSS base score of the finding, as shown in the table below. The clock starts when the finding is first reported.
Severity | CVSS score | Deadline
Critical | 9.0 to 10.0 | 7 days
High | 7.0 to 8.9 | 30 days
Medium | 4.0 to 6.9 | 90 days
Low | 0.1 to 3.9 | 180 days
A vulnerability listed in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog is treated as Critical regardless of its CVSS score and must be remediated within 72 hours on internet-facing systems.

4. Exceptions
Risk acceptance requests require approval from the Risk Owner and the CISO. An accepted risk is valid for 6 months and must then be renewed. Expired acceptances reopen the finding automatically.

5. Governance and Metrics
The Vulnerability Management Lead chairs a review meeting every Tuesday at 10:00. The target is to keep overdue Critical findings at zero and overdue High findings below 5 percent.

6. Roles and Responsibilities
The Vulnerability Management Lead runs the scanning program and reports to the SOC Manager. Asset owners are responsible for fixing findings on their systems within the deadlines. The Server Team and the Endpoint Team apply patches, and the Risk Owner decides whether a residual risk can be accepted.

7. Definitions
CVSS, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, rates the technical severity of a vulnerability from 0.0 to 10.0. A finding is a single vulnerability on a single asset. A compensating control is a safeguard that reduces the risk of a vulnerability that cannot be patched immediately, such as network isolation or a virtual patch.

8. Related Documents
Related documents are the Patch Management Policy (AIT-IR-PM-008) and the Log Management and Retention Policy (AIT-IR-LG-006).

PATCH MANAGEMENT POLICY (SYNTHETIC)
===================================

SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. PURPOSE AND RESPONSIBILITIES

This policy describes how AIT keeps operating systems and applications up to date. Timely patching removes the weaknesses that attackers most often exploit. The policy has document ID AIT-IR-PM-008 and is at version 1.3. The Endpoint Team owns the patching process for workstations and the Server Team owns patching for servers.

2. ROUTINE PATCHING

Routine patches are deployed in a monthly window on the second Wednesday of each month between 01:00 and 05:00. Maintenance notices are sent 5 days before each window so that departments can plan around them.

Patches are first deployed to a pilot group of 50 test devices and observed for 72 hours before wider rollout. A rollback plan must exist before any deployment and rollback must be possible within 2 hours.

3. EMERGENCY PATCHING

Emergency patches for actively exploited vulnerabilities are deployed within 48 hours. Emergency patches need approval from the Change Advisory Board chair, while routine patches are pre-approved as standard changes.

4. SERVERS AND APPLICATIONS

Domain controllers are patched in two waves, and the second wave starts at least 24 hours after the first wave, so that a faulty patch cannot take down all of them at once.

Browsers and PDF readers are updated automatically within 7 days of release. Network device firmware is reviewed quarterly.

5. USERS AND EXCEPTIONS

Users may postpone a required reboot at most 3 times, for a maximum of 24 hours in total.

Backup and Restore Standard (SYNTHETIC)
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. Purpose
This standard defines how AIT protects its data with backups so that systems can be restored after hardware failure, human error, or a malicious attack. It has document ID AIT-IR-BR-009 and is at version 1.5. It follows the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of data, on two different media types, with one copy kept offsite.

2. Schedule and Protection
Daily incremental backups run at 23:00 and weekly full backups run on Sundays at 01:00. Backups are encrypted with AES-256 both in transit and at rest.
Daily backups are kept for 35 days, weekly backups for 12 weeks, monthly backups for 12 months, and yearly backups for 7 years.

3. Offsite and Offline Copies
Monthly tapes are rotated to a contracted offsite facility every 30 days. The facility is located 40 km from the main campus. The offline vault is a fireproof safe in Building C.
Backup repositories are immutable for 30 days. Deleting a backup before that period ends requires two administrators.

4. Administration
Backup administrators use a separate identity domain and hardware security tokens, so that a compromise of the main directory does not expose the backups. A failed backup job creates a ticket within 15 minutes. Two consecutive failures of the same job raise the ticket to priority P2.

5. Recovery Objectives
Systems are grouped into tiers. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss and the recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable downtime.

6. Restore Testing
Restore tests are performed every quarter and at least 10 randomly selected systems must be restored. A restore test passes only when the data is verified within 4 hours. Failed tests are reported to the CISO.

7. Roles and Responsibilities
The Storage Team operates the backup platform and owns the backup schedule. Service owners assign their systems to a recovery tier and approve restore test results. The CISO receives reports of failed restore tests and decides on corrective actions.

8. Definitions
An incremental backup copies only data that changed since the previous backup, while a full backup copies all selected data. An immutable backup cannot be altered or deleted until its lock period ends. A recovery tier is a group of systems that share the same recovery objectives.

EDR Alert Triage Procedure (SYNTHETIC)
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT: This document is fictional and was created for the APA Secure Incident Knowledge Assistant project. The Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) does not exist.

1. Purpose
This procedure explains how the SOC triages SentryEDR alerts. Consistent triage keeps response times predictable and reduces the number of real threats that are missed. It has document ID AIT-IR-ED-010 and is at version 1.0. SentryEDR assigns each alert a risk score from 0 to 100.

2. Severity and Acknowledgement
Scores of 80 and above are Critical, scores from 60 to 79 are High, scores from 40 to 59 are Medium, and scores below 40 are Low. Critical alerts must be acknowledged within 5 minutes, High alerts within 15 minutes, Medium alerts within 60 minutes, and Low alerts within 8 business hours.

3. Triage Steps
The analyst reviews the process tree, the parent process, and the user context of every alert. The file hash is checked against the internal allowlist and two threat intelligence feeds.
Tier 1 may isolate a workstation without further approval when the risk score is 90 or higher. Tier 1 escalates to Tier 2 after 20 minutes without a confident verdict.

4. Closing Alerts
An alert with a score of 60 or higher may be closed as a false positive only after a second analyst reviews it. Triage notes must include the alert ID, host name, user, and verdict. Notes are added to the ticket within 10 minutes of closing the alert.

5. Automation and Tuning
SentryEDR terminates processes automatically only for the rule set named Block-Known-Bad. All other rules only raise alerts. Detection rules with a false-positive rate above 30 percent over 14 days are reviewed for tuning.

6. Queue and Sensor Health

Tier 1 analysts perform first-line triage. Tier 2 analysts handle escalations, tune detection rules, and run threat hunts. The SOC Manager reviews queue metrics every week, and the Endpoint Team repairs or reinstalls sensors that fail health checks.

publisher: APA Project (synthetic document)
text:
AIT Incident Severity and Escalation Matrix
Document ID: AIT-IR-STD-011 | Version: 2.1 | Owner: SOC Manager | Effective date: 1 February 2026 | Review cycle: annual

1. Purpose and Scope
This standard defines how the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) rates the seriousness of a security incident and who must be told. A consistent rating ensures that response effort, staffing and notification are proportionate to the risk.
It applies to all AIT employees, contractors and systems, including the research network, the student network and cloud services operated on behalf of AIT.

2. Definitions
Incident: a confirmed or suspected event that threatens the confidentiality, integrity or availability of AIT information or systems.
Severity: a rating from 1 to 4, where Severity 1 is the most serious.
Duty Officer: the SOC analyst who is on shift and holds the incident pager.
Incident Commander (IC): the person with overall authority for a declared incident, appointed by the SOC Manager.
Acknowledgement: a recorded response to a page or alert showing that a named person has taken ownership.

3. Severity Levels
Severity 1 (Critical): ransomware encryption on any production server, confirmed compromise of the student records system, or confirmed theft of regulated personal data. A named responder must acknowledge within 15 minutes and a status update is posted to the incident channel every 30 minutes.
Severity 2 (High): malware confirmed on more than 5 endpoints, or compromise of a privileged account with no evidence of data loss. Acknowledgement is required within 30 minutes and status updates are posted every 2 hours.
Severity 3 (Medium): malware on a single endpoint that EDR has already contained, or a phishing email that was clicked without credentials being entered. Acknowledgement is required within 4 hours and updates are posted once per day.

text:
Severity 3 (Medium): malware on a single endpoint that EDR has already contained, or a phishing email that was clicked without credentials being entered. Acknowledgement is required within 4 hours and updates are posted once per day.
Severity 4 (Low): policy violations, blocked scans and unsuccessful phishing attempts. These are acknowledged by the next business day and have no scheduled updates.

4. Escalation Paths
For Severity 1, the Duty Officer pages the SOC Manager and the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) immediately. The CISO informs the Vice President for Operations within 1 hour.
For Severity 2, the Duty Officer notifies the SOC Manager, and the CISO is informed within 4 hours.
Severity 3 incidents are handled by the on-call analyst, who sends a weekly summary to the SOC Manager. Severity 4 events are logged in the ticketing system only.

5. Escalation Timeouts
If the SOC Manager does not acknowledge a page within 10 minutes, the Duty Officer pages the Deputy SOC Manager. If there is still no acknowledgement after a further 10 minutes, the Duty Officer pages the CISO directly.

6. Upgrading and Downgrading
Any analyst may propose an upgrade at any time. Only the Incident Commander may approve a downgrade, and a downgrade from Severity 1 also requires the concurrence of the CISO.
Severity is reviewed at every status update. When the evidence fits two levels equally well, the higher level applies until the evidence supports a lower one.

7. Related Documents
Notification of users, regulators and the media is governed by the AIT Incident Communications Plan. A post-incident review is mandatory for Severity 1 and Severity 2 incidents and optional for Severity 3 and 4, as described in the AIT Post-Incident Review Template.
Paging and shift arrangements are described in the AIT On-Call and Shift Handover Procedure.

8. Version History
2.1 (1 February 2026): added escalation timeouts and the Deputy SOC Manager.
2.0 (3 March 2025): replaced three severity levels with four.
1.0 (10 June 2023): first release.

AIT Incident Communications Plan
Document ID: AIT-IR-PLN-012 | Version: 1.4 | Owner: Director of Communications and CISO | Effective date: 15 January 2026 | Review cycle: annual

1. Purpose
This plan sets out who communicates during a security incident at the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT), with whom, in what form and by what deadline. Its aim is to keep every audience accurately informed without disclosing details that would help an attacker or breach confidentiality.

2. Roles
Communications Lead: drafts all messages and keeps the communications log. This role is assigned by the Incident Commander when a Severity 1 or Severity 2 incident is declared.
Legal Counsel: reviews every external message and is the only contact with regulators and law enforcement.
Data Protection Officer (DPO): decides whether an incident is a personal data breach that must be notified.
Help Desk Lead: distributes approved notices to affected users and handles their questions.
Director of Communications: the only person permitted to speak to the media.

3. Principles
One source of truth: every statement comes from the incident ticket, not from memory or rumor.
Need to know: technical indicators and system names are shared only inside the response team.
No speculation: messages state what is confirmed, what is suspected and when the next update will come.
No blame: messages never name individuals or suppliers as the cause.

4. Audiences and Deadlines
Response team: the Communications Lead opens the dedicated chat channel named ir-bridge within 10 minutes of a Severity 1 or Severity 2 declaration.
Executive leadership: for Severity 1, the first briefing is given within 1 hour of declaration, followed by briefings every 4 hours until containment.
Affected users: the Help Desk Lead sends a notice written in plain language, without technical indicators.

text:
AIT POST-INCIDENT REVIEW TEMPLATE
=================================

Document ID: AIT-IR-TPL-013 | Version: 1.2 | Owner: SOC Manager | Effective date: 12 February 2026

1. Purpose
----------

A post-incident review (PIR) turns an incident into lasting improvement. This template standardises how the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) records what happened, why it happened and what will change.

2. Ground Rules
---------------

- Blameless: the review examines processes, tools and decisions, never the personal fault of individuals.
- A PIR is mandatory for Severity 1 and Severity 2 incidents. For Severity 1 the review meeting is held within 5 business days of incident closure, and for Severity 2 within 10 business days.
- The meeting is led by a facilitator who was not the Incident Commander for the incident.
- Required attendees: the Incident Commander, the responders involved, the owner of each affected system and a representative of the Help Desk.

3. Template Sections
--------------------

Section 1 - Summary: two to three sentences describing the incident, its severity and its outcome, written for a non-technical reader.

Section 2 - Timeline: key events in UTC, including first malicious activity, detection, declaration, containment, eradication and recovery.

Section 3 - Detection: how the incident was found and whether an existing control should have found it sooner.

Section 4 - Impact: affected systems, number of users, data involved, downtime in hours and estimated cost.

publisher: APA Project (synthetic document)
text:
Section 3 - Detection: how the incident was found and whether an existing control should have found it sooner.

Section 4 - Impact: affected systems, number of users, data involved, downtime in hours and estimated cost.

Section 5 - Root Cause: the underlying cause, found by asking why repeatedly until a process or control gap is identified; the 5 Whys method is recommended.

Section 6 - What Went Well: practices and tools that worked and should be kept.

Section 7 - What Went Poorly: delays, gaps and surprises.

Section 8 - Action Items: each item has an owner, a due date and a priority.

4. Metrics
----------

- MTTD (mean time to detect): time from first malicious activity to detection.
- MTTC (mean time to contain): time from detection to containment.
- MTTR (mean time to recover): time from detection to full restoration of service.

5. Action Items and Publication
-------------------------------

Action items must be due within 30 days unless the SOC Manager approves a longer period. Overdue items are reported at the monthly security review.

The final report is published within 15 business days of the meeting. It is stored in the restricted incident repository and retained for 7 years.

6. Version History
------------------

- 1.1 (18 September 2025): added the facilitator rule.

text:
AIT Chain of Custody and Evidence Handling Checklist
Document ID: AIT-IR-CHK-014 | Version: 1.3 | Owner: Digital Forensics Lead | Effective date: 9 March 2026

1. Purpose
This checklist ensures that digital and physical evidence collected during an incident at the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) remains authentic and admissible. Every person who handles evidence must be recorded from collection to disposal.

2. Roles
Collector: the analyst who gathers the evidence.
Evidence Custodian: the person responsible for the evidence room and the evidence server, and the keeper of all custody forms.
Legal Counsel: places and releases legal holds.

3. Before Collection
Obtain approval from the Incident Commander. A running system must not be powered off without this approval.
Record the date, time, time zone and the offset between the system clock and a trusted time source.
Photograph the scene, screen and connected cables where physical devices are involved.
Assign a unique evidence ID in the format AIT-EV-YYYY-NNNN.

4. Order of Collection
Evidence is collected from the most volatile source to the least volatile: memory first, then network connections and running processes, then disk, and finally logs and backups.

5. Imaging and Integrity
Use a hardware write blocker when imaging a physical disk.
Calculate a SHA-256 hash before and after imaging, and record both values on the custody form.
Create two copies of every image: a master copy that is never opened, and a working copy used for analysis.

6. Packaging and Transfer
Seal physical items in tamper-evident bags and label them with the evidence ID, collector name and time.
Every transfer is recorded on the custody form with the names and signatures of both parties, the date and time, and the reason for the transfer.

AIT ON-CALL AND SHIFT HANDOVER PROCEDURE
========================================

Document ID: AIT-IR-PRC-015 | Version: 1.5 | Owner: SOC Manager | Effective date: 2 March 2026

1. Purpose
----------

This procedure keeps the Security Operations Center (SOC) of the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) staffed around the clock and makes sure no incident information is lost when responsibility changes hands.

2. Shifts
---------

The SOC operates 24 hours a day in three 8-hour shifts: 08:00 to 16:00, 16:00 to 24:00 and 00:00 to 08:00 local time.

3. On-Call Rota
---------------

- The on-call rota is weekly and changes on Monday at 09:00 local time.
- Each week has a primary and a secondary on-call analyst.
- On-call analysts must be able to reach a secure workstation within 45 minutes.
- No analyst is on call for more than one week in three.
- Rota swaps must be agreed at least 48 hours in advance and recorded in the rota.

4. Paging
---------

Pages are sent only for Severity 1 and Severity 2 incidents. The on-call analyst must acknowledge a page within 15 minutes.

If the primary does not acknowledge within 15 minutes, the paging system alerts the secondary automatically. If neither acknowledges within a further 10 minutes, the Duty Officer calls the SOC Manager.

5. Rest After Call-Outs

-----------------------

After a call-out that lasts more than 4 hours between 22:00 and 06:00, the analyst receives at least 11 hours of rest before the next shift.

6. Shift Handover
-----------------

The outgoing and incoming analysts hold a live handover of about 15 minutes at the start of every shift. A handover by message alone is not accepted.

The handover note must list the following items:

- all open incidents with their severity
- pending actions with their owners
- watch items, such as suspicious hosts under observation

7. On-Call Kit and Contacts
---------------------------

Each on-call analyst carries a company laptop, a phone with the paging application and a hardware security token. Passwords and recovery codes are never written in handover notes.

Emergency contact numbers are kept in the on-call directory, which is reviewed on the first business day of each month.

text:
AIT Web Server Compromise and Webshell Response Playbook
Document ID: AIT-IR-PBK-016 | Version: 1.1 | Owner: Web Platform Owner and SOC Manager | Effective date: 10 November 2026

1. Purpose and Scope
This playbook describes how the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) responds when a web server is suspected or confirmed to be compromised, in particular when an attacker has planted a webshell. A webshell is a script uploaded to a web server that lets an attacker run commands through a web request.
The playbook covers all internet-facing web servers operated by or for AIT.

2. Roles
Incident Commander (IC): appointed by the SOC Manager and approves every containment action.
Web Platform Owner: the engineer responsible for the affected site, who rebuilds and patches the server.
Forensics Analyst: captures and preserves evidence following the Chain of Custody and Evidence Handling Checklist.

3. Indicators
New or modified script files in the web root that do not match a deployment record.
The web server process starting command interpreters such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe or /bin/sh.
Repeated POST requests to a rarely used script file from a single external IP address.
Outbound connections from the web server to unknown destinations.

4. Severity
A confirmed webshell on any internet-facing server is rated Severity 2 under the Incident Severity and Escalation Matrix. It is raised to Severity 1 if the server holds or can reach the student records system.

5. Containment
The web server is isolated within 60 minutes of confirmation by removing it from the load balancer pool and moving it to the quarantine VLAN. The server must not be powered off, because memory evidence would be lost.

The webshell must not be deleted until the Forensics Analyst has copied the web root and captured memory.

6. Investigation
Review web access logs backward from the first request to the webshell to find the initial entry point.
Check for persistence such as new scheduled tasks, new local accounts and changed startup scripts.
Search other servers for the same file hash and for requests from the same attacker address.

7. Eradication and Recovery
Rebuild the server from a known-good image; cleaning a compromised server in place is not permitted.
Restore website content from a backup taken before the earliest confirmed compromise time.
Rotate every credential and key that the server could read, including database passwords, API tokens and TLS private keys.
Patch or remove the vulnerable component before the server returns to production.

8. Post-Recovery Monitoring
After the server returns to production, the SOC monitors it with enhanced logging for 30 days. A post-incident review is held in line with the Post-Incident Review Template.

9. Version History
1.1 (10 November 2026): added the rule against cleaning in place.
1.0 (22 June 2025): first release.

AIT Email Security Standard
Document ID: AIT-SEC-STD-017 | Version: 1.3 | Owner: Messaging Security Engineer | Effective date: 5 October 2026

1. Purpose
This standard sets the minimum technical controls that protect email at the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) against spoofing, phishing and malware delivery. The handling of phishing emails that reach users is covered by the Phishing Incident Response Procedure.

2. Domain Authentication
SPF: every AIT sending domain publishes an SPF record, and the record must end in -all.
DKIM: all outbound mail is signed with 2048-bit keys, and keys are rotated every 12 months.
DMARC: the policy for every AIT domain must be p=reject. A new domain may use p=quarantine for at most 90 days before moving to p=reject.
Parked domains that never send mail publish a null SPF record and p=reject.

3. Inbound Filtering
Messages from outside AIT carry the tag [EXTERNAL] in the subject line.
Executable and script attachments (.exe, .js, .vbs, .scr, .bat) are blocked at the gateway.
Archive files protected with a password are quarantined because they cannot be scanned.
Office documents with macros from external senders are quarantined.
Links in inbound email are rewritten so that the destination is checked at the time of the click.

4. Quarantine
Quarantined messages are kept for 21 days and then deleted automatically. Users may request release of a message, but messages classified as malware can only be released by the SOC.

5. Mailbox Rules and Forwarding
Automatic forwarding of mail to external addresses is disabled for all mailboxes.

text:
AIT NETWORK SEGMENTATION STANDARD
=================================

Document ID: AIT-SEC-STD-018 | Version: 1.2 | Owner: Network Security Manager | Effective date: 20 September 2026

1. Purpose
----------

This standard defines the network zones of the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) and the rules for traffic between them, so that a compromise in one zone does not spread freely to others.

2. Zones
--------

- DMZ: internet-facing web, mail gateway and reverse proxy servers.
- Corporate: staff workstations and office printers.
- Student: student devices and campus Wi-Fi.
- Research: research clusters and lab equipment.
- Server: production application and database servers, including the student records system.
- Management: hypervisors, backup servers and network device management interfaces.
- Building: building control and physical access systems.

3. Traffic Rules
----------------

- Traffic between zones is denied by default; only flows listed in the firewall rule base are allowed.
- DMZ servers may not initiate connections into the Corporate or Student zones.
- The Student zone has no direct access to the Server zone.
- The Management zone is reachable only from the jump hosts, and jump host logins require multi-factor authentication.
- Servers may initiate outbound internet connections only to destinations on an approved allow list.
- The Building zone has no route to the internet.

4. Rule Governance
------------------

title: Network Segmentation Standard (SYNTHETIC)
publisher: APA Project (synthetic document)
text:
- Servers may initiate outbound internet connections only to destinations on an approved allow list.
- The Building zone has no route to the internet.

4. Rule Governance
------------------

Every firewall rule has a named owner, a written justification and an expiry date. Temporary rules last at most 30 days. Research zone exceptions last at most 12 months.

All rules are reviewed every 6 months, and rules that are not re-approved at the review are removed.

5. Emergency Isolation
----------------------

During an incident the SOC may move a host to the quarantine VLAN, VLAN 999, without prior approval. The SOC informs the Incident Commander within 30 minutes of the move.

VLAN 999 permits traffic only to the SOC investigation host.

6. Definitions
--------------

- Zone: a group of systems with a similar level of trust and function, separated from other groups by a firewall.
- Jump host: a hardened server that is the only path administrators may use to reach the Management zone.
- Firewall rule base: the complete list of permitted flows between zones, maintained by the Network Security Team.
- Quarantine VLAN: an isolated network segment used to contain a host that is suspected to be compromised.

7. Roles and Exceptions
-----------------------

The Network Security Manager owns the firewall rule base. System owners request new rules and re-approve their own rules at each review. The SOC applies emergency isolation but does not change the rule base.

Requests for exceptions to this standard are sent to the Network Security Manager and need the approval of the CISO.

AIT Supplier Incident Notification Standard
Document ID: AIT-SEC-STD-019 | Version: 1.0 | Owner: Vendor Manager and CISO | Effective date: 1 October 2026

1. Purpose
This standard sets out what suppliers must tell the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) when a security incident affects AIT data or services, and what AIT does after it is told.

2. Supplier Tiers
Tier 1 (critical): suppliers that process student records, host production systems or hold administrator access to AIT networks.
Tier 2 (important): suppliers that handle other AIT personal data or provide services whose outage would stop teaching or research.
Tier 3 (standard): all other suppliers.

3. Definitions
Supplier: any external organization that provides goods or services to AIT, including cloud and software providers.
Supplier incident: a confirmed or suspected event that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of AIT data or services held by the supplier.
Awareness: the moment any employee of the supplier recognises that an incident may have occurred, not the moment its investigation is complete.

4. Notification Deadlines
A Tier 1 supplier must notify AIT within 12 hours of becoming aware of an incident. Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers must notify AIT within 24 hours.
Notification is made by phone to the SOC duty line and by email to the SOC mailbox. A notification to an account manager or a help desk does not count.

5. Content of the Initial Notification
what happened and when it was discovered
which AIT data, systems or users are affected
actions already taken to contain the incident
a named contact who is reachable 24 hours a day

6. Updates and Final Report
The supplier sends an update every 2 business days until the incident is closed. A final report with root cause and corrective actions is due within 30 days of closure.

7. Roles

AIT Security Awareness Training Program
Document ID: AIT-SEC-PRG-020 | Version: 1.2 | Owner: Security Awareness Manager | Effective date: 1 September 2026

1. Purpose
This program defines the security awareness training that every member of the Aurelian Institute of Technology (AIT) must complete and how its effectiveness is measured.

2. Definitions and Roles
Core awareness course: the introductory online course on phishing, passwords, data handling and incident reporting. It takes about 40 minutes.
Phishing simulation: a harmless test email sent by the Security Awareness Manager to measure how staff respond.
Security Awareness Manager: runs the program, owns the course content and reports its results.
Line managers: make sure their teams finish training by the deadline.
Human Resources: tells the Security Awareness Manager when new employees and contractors start.

3. Audiences and Frequency
New employees and contractors complete the core awareness course within 30 days of their start date.
All staff complete a refresher course every 12 months.
New students complete a 20-minute orientation module in their first week.
Privileged users, such as system administrators, complete additional role-based training every year.
Senior leaders receive a security briefing twice a year.

4. Phishing Simulations
The Security Awareness Manager runs a phishing simulation for all staff every quarter. The target click rate is below 5 percent and the target reporting rate is above 60 percent. Simulation results are never used for disciplinary action.
Staff who click on 3 simulated phishing emails within 12 months receive one-to-one coaching from the Security Awareness Manager.

5. Compliance
Overdue training is escalated to the line manager 14 days after the deadline. At 45 days after the deadline, access to non-essential systems may be restricted until the training is complete.

6. Content
Course content is reviewed every year and updated with lessons from AIT incidents.

title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)
text:
Overview
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of
Investigation (FBI), and the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)
are releasing this joint distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack guidance for federal, state,
local, tribal, and territorial government entities to serve as a comprehensive resource to
address the specific needs and challenges faced by government agencies in defending
against DDoS attacks.
Distributed denial-of-service attacks typically originate from multiple sources, making them
difficult to trace and effectively block the attacking internet protocol (IP) addresses. This
guide provides an overview of the denial-of-service (DoS) and DDoS landscapes, including
attack types, motivations, and potential impacts on government operations, as well as
practical steps on implementing preventative measures, and incident response for each of
the defined DDoS and DoS technique types. Additionally, it highlights why it is important for
organizations to focus their planning efforts on emerging DDoS trends and technologies to
better defend against malicious DDoS activity.
DoS and DDoS
A DoS and a DDoS attack are similar in that they both aim to disrupt the availability of a
target system or network. However, there are key differences between the two.
1. D
oS Attack: A DoS attack involves a single source used to overwhelm the target
system with a flood of traffic or resource-consuming requests. The malicious actor
typically uses one computer or a small number of computers to generate the attack.
The goal of a DoS attack is to render the target system unavailable to its intended
users and deny them access to resources or services.
2. D
DoS Attack: A DDoS attack involves multiple sources. Often, a multitude of
compromised computers—known as botnets—are coordinated to launch the attack.

title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)
text:
The goal of a DoS attack is to render the target system unavailable to its intended
users and deny them access to resources or services.
2. D
DoS Attack: A DDoS attack involves multiple sources. Often, a multitude of
compromised computers—known as botnets—are coordinated to launch the attack.
Each machine in the botnet sends a flood of traffic or requests to the target system
simultaneously to amplify the follow-on impact. Due to the distributed nature of a
DDoS attack, defending targeted networks has increased difficulty compared to a
DoS attack.
T
he main advantage of a DDoS attack over a DoS attack is the ability to generate a
significantly higher volume of traffic, overwhelming the target system’s resources to a
greater extent. DDoS attacks can also employ various techniques, such as IP spoofing,
which involves a malicious actor manipulating the source IP address and botnets to disguise
the origin of the attack and make it more difficult to trace it back to them.
In terms of impact, both DoS and DDoS attacks can disrupt the availability of a targeted
system or network, leading to service outages, financial losses, and reputational damage.

1. Volume-Based Attacks: These attacks aim to consume the available bandwidth or
system resources of the target by overwhelming it with a massive volume of traffic.
The goal is to saturate the network or exhaust the target’s resources, rendering it
unable to handle legitimate requests.

text:
What Steps Should Your Organization Take Before Experiencing a
DDoS Attack?
No organization can predict when a DDoS attack will occur. However, malicious actors often
look for gaps in security systems to launch a DDoS attack; therefore, it is imperative that an
organization’s network defenders implement best practices to minimize the potential
damage of a DDoS attack. The following is a list of proactive DDoS steps to consider:
1. Risk Assessment: Conduct a thorough and proactive risk assessment to determine
your organizations vulnerability to DDoS attacks. Risk assessments can identify
potential vulnerabilities in your network infrastructure, systems, and applications.
Such an assessment will also help your organization understand the potential impact
of a DDoS attack and aid in prioritizing and implementing appropriate security
measures.
2. Network Monitoring: Implement robust network monitoring tools and intrusion
detection systems (IDS) to identify any unusual or suspicious traffic patterns. This
can heighten your organization’s ability to detect and respond to DDoS attacks.
3. Traffic Analysis: Regularly analyze your network traffic to establish a baseline of
normal traffic patterns. This helps you identify any significant deviations during an
attack.
4. Implement Captcha: Integrating a Captcha challenge into a website or online service
to help differentiate between human users and automated bots, which helps prevent
DDoS attacks. By requiring human interaction to access or interact with websites,
Captcha acts as preventive barrier against DDoS attacks.
5. Incident Response Plan: Develop a comprehensive incident response plan that
outlines the steps to be taken in the event of a DDoS attack. The plan should include
roles and responsibilities, communication channels, and predefined mitigation
strategies.
6. DDoS Mitigation Service: Consider employing the services of a DDoS mitigation
provider.

roles and responsibilities, communication channels, and predefined mitigation
strategies.
6. DDoS Mitigation Service: Consider employing the services of a DDoS mitigation
provider. They possess the expertise and specialized infrastructure to handle largescale attacks and can help filter out malicious traffic before it reaches your network.
7. Bandwidth Capacity Planning: Evaluate your current bandwidth capacity and consider
increasing it to handle sudden spikes in traffic during an attack. This can help
minimize the impact on legitimate users.
8. Load Balancing: Implement load balancing solutions to distribute traffic across
multiple servers or data centers. This can help distribute the load and prevent a
single point of failure during an attack.
9. Firewall Configuration: Configure your firewalls to filter out suspicious traffic patterns
and/or block traffic from known malicious IP addresses. Keep the firewall rules
updated and consider implementing rate limitations to prevent overwhelming traffic.

text:
10. Patch and Update Systems: Regularly update and patch all software, operating
systems, and network devices to address known vulnerabilities. Vulnerable systems
can be exploited to amplify the impact of a DDoS attack.
11. Web Application Security: Implement secure coding practices and conduct regular
security assessments of your web applications. Vulnerable applications can be
targeted to exhaust server resources during an attack.
12. Redundancy and Failover: Implement redundant network infrastructure and ensure
failover mechanisms are in place. This will help maintain service availability during an
attack by quickly redirecting traffic to alternative resources.
13. Employee Awareness and Training: Educate employees about DDoS attacks, their
impact, and how to recognize and report suspicious activities. This will help minimize
the risk of falling victim to social engineering attacks that can aid in launching a
DDoS attack.
14. Communication Plan: Develop a communication plan to keep stakeholders informed
during an attack. This includes internal teams, customers, and third-party service
providers. Clear communication helps manage expectations and coordinates
response efforts.
15. Backup and Recovery: Regularly back up critical data and ensure you have a tested
and updated disaster recovery plan. This will help you recover quickly after an attack
and minimize potential data loss.
Note: These steps can help mitigate the impact of a DDoS attack, it's crucial for organizations to
remain vigilant to these types of attacks and remain in constant communication with their
organization cybersecurity professionals and stay updated on the latest security practices to
effectively defend against evolving threats.

publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)
text:
How Does Your Organization Know If It’s Experiencing a DDoS
Attack?
Identifying whether your organizations is experiencing a DDoS attack can be challenging, as
symptoms can vary depending on the attack type and intensity. The following is a wideranging list to help network defenders determine if there is a DDoS attack occurring:
1. Website or Service Unavailability: The most common symptom of a DDoS attack is
the unavailability of a website or online service. If a website suddenly becomes
inaccessible or experiences significant slowdowns, it could be a sign of a DDoS
attack.
2. Network Congestion: If there is a sudden increase in network traffic or congestion, it
may indicate a DDoS attack. Network monitoring tools, or bandwidth usage reports
can help identify abnormal spikes in traffic.
3. Unusual Traffic Patterns: Look for unusual traffic patterns in network logs or
monitoring systems. This can include a significant increase in requests from specific
IP addresses or a high volume of traffic targeting a specific resource or URL.
4. Server or Application Crashes: DDoS attacks can overwhelm your servers or
applications, leading to crashes or unresponsiveness. If networks suffer from
frequent server or application failures without an apparent reason, it could be a sign
of an attack.
5. High Resource Utilization: Monitor server and network resource utilization metrics,
such as CPU usage, memory consumption, or bandwidth usage. A sudden and
sustained increase in resource consumption may indicate a DDoS attack.
6. Inability To Access Other Network Services: Websites or services may not be the only
target of a DDoS attack, other critical network infrastructure components (such as
DNS servers or firewalls) may also be at risk. If there are difficulties associated with
accessing these services, it could be a sign of an attack.
7. Anomalies in User Behavior: Monitor user behavior on your website or service.
section: 14. Communication Plan: Develop a communication plan to keep stakeholders informed

title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)
text:
If there are difficulties associated with
accessing these services, it could be a sign of an attack.
7. Anomalies in User Behavior: Monitor user behavior on your website or service. If
there is a significant increase in the number of requests from a single IP address or
unusual patterns, it may be a sign of a DDoS attack.
8. Flood of Spam or Malicious Emails: DDoS attacks can be launched in conjunction
with other types of attacks, such as email spam campaigns. If there is a sudden
surge in spam or malicious emails originating from organizational networks, it could
be part of a coordinated DDoS attack.
9. Notifications From DDoS Protection Service: If you have engaged a DDoS protection
service, they may proactively alert you if they detect an ongoing attack on your
network.
section: 4. Server or Application Crashes: DDoS attacks can overwhelm your servers or

title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
publisher: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)
text:
10. Communication Disruptions: DDoS attacks can target communication channels, such
as Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) services or messaging platforms. If there are
disruptions or quality degradation in network communication services, it may be an
indication of an attack.
How Organizations Can Respond to a DDoS Incident
Organizations experiencing a DDoS attack, are encouraged to initiate incident response
plans, contact DDoS protection service provider (if applicable), and engage with your
network security team to mitigate the attack and restore normal operations. The following is
a list of steps to consider:
1. Identify the Attack: Recognize the signs of a DDoS attack, such as a sudden surge in
traffic, increased network latency, or unavailability of services. Use network
monitoring tools and traffic analysis to confirm the attack.
2. Activate Incident Response Plan: Implement your organization’s documented and
approved incident response plan immediately. This plan should outline the roles and
responsibilities of key personnel, communication channels, and the steps to be taken
during a DDoS attack.
3. Notify Service Providers: Contact internet service providers (ISP) or hosting providers
to inform them about the attack. They may have mitigation measures in place or be
able to reroute traffic to help mitigate the impact.
4. Gather Evidence: Document and collect as much information as possible about the
attack, including timestamps, IP addresses, packet captures, and any logs or alerts
generated by your network infrastructure. This evidence can be useful for reporting
the incident to law enforcement agencies or for future analysis.
5. Implement Traffic Filtering: Configure network infrastructure, firewalls, or intrusion
prevention systems to filter out malicious traffic. Use rate-limitation or access control
lists to block traffic from suspicious IP addresses or specific protocols commonly
used in DDoS attacks.

6. Enable DDoS Mitigation Services: If available, activate DDoS mitigation services
provided by your ISP or third-party vendors specializing in DDoS protection. These
services can help filter and divert malicious traffic, allowing legitimate traffic to reach
your network.
7. Scale Up Bandwidth and Resources: If your organization has the capacity, consider
scaling up your network bandwidth and resources to absorb the attack traffic. This
may involve adding additional servers or increasing your network capacity
temporarily.
8. Enable Content Delivery Network (CDN): Utilize a CDN service to distribute content
across multiple servers and data centers geographically. CDNs can help mitigate
DDoS attacks by absorbing and distributing traffic, minimizing the impact on your
infrastructure.
